newsitem.title: USA: Intel unveils new multimedia chip.
newsitem.headline: Intel unveils new multimedia chip.

text.p: Intel Corp. Wednesday unveiled its anxiously awaited new multimedia computer chip, which brings TV-quality video, three-dimensional graphics and better sound to personal computers.
At the same time, about 20 PC makers and 19 software companies announced products using the MMX Pentium chip, many saying they expected the new technology to boost sales.
"A lot of people have been waiting for technology to develop so the PC is like the TV experience. This is it," said Leo Rossi, vice president of software company Highway One Media Entertainment Inc.

Industry analysts said the new chip will quickly become the new standard for the industry, allowing Intel to maintain its dominance over the semiconductor market and force other PC component makers to cut prices.
An executive with Micron Electronics Inc., which sells PCs by phone, said the company was receiving an "enormous" number of calls about its new MMX PC.
Compaq Computer Corp., the leading maker of PCs in the world, also announced PCs based on the new chip, as did International Business Machines Corp., Dell Computer Corp. and Gateway 2000.
However, many analysts said the chip -- a Pentium with so-called MMX or multimedia extensions built in -- won't help PC sales in the short term, but might over a longer time.
"I don't think it will be a quick fix to retail PC market demand," Charles Boucher of brokerage UBS Securities said. "But over the long term it will bring in new users."

He and others said more software created for the chip would be needed in the retail market to fuel sales of the machines. A Bear Stearns & Co. brokerage analyst said the introduction of the new chip might even slow January PC sales as consumers evaluated their options.

Santa Clara, Calif.-based Intel said its aim with the MMX was to persuade more consumers to buy PCs by making the personal computer more fun to use. The more PCs sold, the more processors Intel sells.

"Our whole goal here is to deliver a new level of performance and capability to the consumer," said Mike Aymar, vice president of Intel's desktop products group, who demonstrated video conferencing and game playing on an MMX machine.
Intel Chief Operating Officer Craig Barrett described the MMX effort as part of the "battle for eyeballs" between the PC and TV industries.
Intel said it planned to convert its entire microprocessor product line to MMX versions within a year or two. That, in turn, will compel other chip makers to march in step.
"The real story here is that this is one more step by Intel toward the total consolidation of added value in the PC," said Cowen & Co. analyst Drew Peck.

"They did it with processors first, then chip sets, then motherboards; now they're doing it with MMX. What Intel wants is 100 percent of the value-added in the PC and so far they've been pretty good at getting there," he said.
Indeed, as the world's largest maker of microprocessors -- the brains of the PC -- Intel already commands tremendous clout in the semiconductor market.

But industry analysts say Intel wants to expand its influence to other areas of the computer, such as modem chips and graphics functions, in order to drive PC prices down while protecting its own profit margins.

By launching the MMX, which can do some of the functions already performed by modem chips and graphics chips, Intel will force supplies of those chips to cut prices, thereby making PCs more affordable.

"The actual impact on MMX is far more subtle than it seems," Peck said. "The way they protect their margins is by taking it out of the hide of other suppliers, not other processor producers, but other suppliers of chips to the PC business."

Intel priced the MMX chip lower than it usually does when introducing a new chip. It priced 166- and 200-megahertz MMX Pentiums for desktop PCs at $407 and $550 per chip in 1,000-unit quantities aimed at PC makers. By comparison, the first Pentium was introduced at about $1,000 per chip in 1,000-unit quantities.
Barrett said the low pricing for MMX chips was needed to allow them to be built into PCs at the "mainstream consumer prices" of $1.500 to $2,000 for a PC.
Intel priced MMX chips for mobile computers at $443 for a 150-megahertz and $550 for a 166-megahertz in 1,000-unit quanties.
